claims.text: For initially solid-solution nanoparticles containing five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios, structural and chemical stability is governed by a coherent nanoparticle–substrate interface.
A coherent nanoparticle–substrate interface maintains the solid-solution structure.
A coherent nanoparticle–substrate interface prevents phase segregation.
The proposed interface-mediated stability applies from 473 to 1923 K.
The proposed interface-mediated stability applies under both catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions.
The nanoparticles initially have a crystallized solid-solution structure.
The experimental intervention is heating under vacuum from 473 to 1923 K.
Nanoparticles having a coherent interface will be compared with nanoparticles lacking a coherent interface.
The coherent-interface nanoparticles are predicted to show a 20% increase in stability relative to the initial baseline.
Stability is operationally measured as retention of the solid-solution structure.
Solid-solution retention will be characterized using X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy.
Energy-dispersive spectroscopy will be used in the controlled experiment.
The hypothesis is declared falsified if nanoparticles without a coherent interface retain at least 10% of the solid-solution structure relative to the initial baseline.
The coherent interface may degrade over time.

contradictions.description: The outcome is framed as a 20% increase in retention relative to the initial solid-solution baseline. If initial retention is the natural 100% reference, a 20% increase is not coherently defined; the intended quantity may instead be a 20-percentage-point advantage over the no-interface control.

The intervention specifies vacuum heating, while the claimed domain is catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions. These environments are not defined as vacuum conditions, so the tested environment does not clearly match the claimed operating domain.

The design calls for a controlled comparison, but the falsification rule uses only an absolute retention threshold for the no-interface group and does not compare it with the coherent-interface group or with the predicted 20% stability difference. Thus it could declare falsification even when the coherent interface provides the predicted benefit.
